lead: This unit gives the hardware and model vocabulary behind parallel and distributed computing. You learn to classify machines, compare shared and distributed memory, reason with PRAM, judge a network, compute speedup and efficiency, and map work to processors. You finish with data versus model parallelism, using a small machine-learning training example.
about: This unit builds the vocabulary for parallel and distributed computing. Chapter 1.1 explains why single processors hit limits and where parallelism appears, from bits to jobs. Chapter 1.2 classifies machines by instruction and data streams, including dataflow. Chapter 1.3 compares shared-memory and distributed-memory hardware. Chapter 1.4 gives the PRAM model and its EREW, CREW and CRCW variants. Chapter 1.5 describes mesh, tree, hypercube and butterfly networks using degree, diameter and bisection width. Chapter 1.6 measures speedup and efficiency with Amdahl's law. Chapter 1.7 turns a problem into tasks and balances them. Chapter 1.8 separates data parallelism from model parallelism, with a machine-learning example. The chapters move from hardware ideas to models to performance and mapping.

chapters.idea: Parallel processing uses many execution units to cut time or handle larger problems, and parallelism appears at several levels from bits to jobs.
chapters.depth: Motivate parallel processing with power and memory walls, instruction-level limits, big data and machine-learning workloads. Connect it to computer components: CPU cores, cache, memory, interconnect and I/O. Define granularity and levels: bit level, instruction level (pipelining, superscalar), data level (vector units, SIMD lanes), task or thread level, and job level. Distinguish parallel computing from distributed computing. Introduce design issues: partitioning, communication, synchronisation, scalability and fault tolerance, then map each to a later chapter or Unit 4. Mention the high-performance ecosystem: multicore CPU, GPU, cluster and cloud, with limits of power, cost and communication.

figure.title: Levels of parallelism
figure.aria: A top-to-bottom ladder from bit-level parallelism through instruction, data and task parallelism to job-level parallelism.

chapters.example: A task has 20% serial work. (a) Maximum speedup with unlimited processors is 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5. (b) With 16 processors and perfect scaling of the remaining 80%, S = 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.8 ÷ 16) = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4. Why is S not 16?
chapters.trap: More cores do not automatically give proportional speedup; the serial part and overhead limit it.
chapters.leave: Detailed speedup formulas to Chapter 6, programming tools to Unit 3, and distributed-system challenges to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Flynn's models classify machines by how many instruction streams and data streams they use at once.
chapters.depth: Define instruction stream and data stream. Cover SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD; explain why MISD is mostly theoretical. For SIMD, describe one control unit, many ALUs, lockstep execution and masks; shared-memory SIMD algorithms mean the same operation on many array elements. For MIMD, describe independent threads or processes, then split into shared-memory and message-passing forms. Explain dataflow: an operation fires when its operands are ready, which is not a Flynn class. Introduce SPMD as a common programming style, not a Flynn class. Use exam wording such as SIMD computer, MIMD multiprocessor and dataflow graph.

figure.aria: A classification tree: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD, and dataflow, with SIMD showing GPU lanes and MIMD splitting into shared-memory and message-passing forms.

chapters.example: Name the Flynn class: (a) a GPU runs one add instruction on 32 lanes; (b) an 8-core CPU runs different programs on each core; (c) a scalar CPU adds two registers; (d) a dataflow adder fires when both inputs arrive. Answer: SIMD, MIMD, SISD, dataflow, which is not a Flynn class.
chapters.trap: Do not call a multicore CPU SIMD just because it has many cores; SIMD needs one instruction over many data items.
chapters.leave: PRAM details to Chapter 4, GPU programming to Unit 3, and dataflow algorithms are not needed here.

chapters.idea: Shared-memory machines give all processors one address space, while distributed-memory machines give each node private memory and require messages.
chapters.depth: Shared memory: processors see one address space. Cover UMA or SMP with bus or crossbar, NUMA with local and remote latency, and mention COMA. State the cache coherence problem in one line. Distributed memory: each node has private memory and nodes communicate by messages; cover clusters, MPP systems and multicore nodes. Compare message passing with shared memory in latency, bandwidth, scalability and programming effort. Name shared-memory SIMD and tree or mesh machines only as architecture forms; details are in Chapter 5. Introduce send and receive primitives, synchronous and asynchronous execution at a basic level; full protocols are in Unit 4.

figure.title: Shared vs distributed
figure.aria: Two memory pictures side by side: four cores connect to one shared RAM block, while two nodes connect to a network.

chapters.example: A job takes 100 s on one core, with 20 s serial. (a) On a 4-core SMP, T4 = 20 + 80 ÷ 4 = 40 s, so S = 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5. (b) On a 2-node cluster, the parallel part splits over 2 nodes and message overhead is 10 s, so T = 20 + 80 ÷ 2 + 10 = 70 s, and S = 100 ÷ 70 ≈ 1.43. Which architecture wins here?
chapters.trap: Shared memory does not mean free communication; remote NUMA access, contention and coherence still cost time.
chapters.leave: Cache coherence protocols and consistency models to Unit 5, MPI and OpenMP to Unit 3, and network topologies to Chapter 5.

chapters.idea: PRAM is an ideal shared-memory model in which many processors run in lockstep and read or write shared cells in unit time.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Define P processors, one shared memory, synchronous steps and unit-cost read or write. Cover EREW, CREW and CRCW; for CRCW, list common, arbitrary and priority conflict rules. Define parallel time and cost as time × processors. Explain simulation between variants: an EREW machine can simulate a CRCW write conflict in O(log P) rounds for many rules by a tree or prefix combine, while a CRCW machine can simulate EREW directly. Stress that PRAM is an ideal model, not real hardware, and has no network delay. Do not derive full algorithms; Unit 2 uses PRAM for algorithm analysis.

figure.aria: Three nested ovals: EREW is the smallest and most restrictive, CREW adds concurrent reads, and CRCW adds concurrent writes with common, arbitrary or priority resolution.

chapters.example: P = 8 processors. In one PRAM step, all 8 write to cell A. Under priority CRCW, the highest-priority write wins in one step. Under EREW, the writes must be ordered; a tree combine needs 3 rounds because log₂ 8 = 3. If each round is 1 time unit and P = 8, cost = 8 × 3 = 24 processor-time units.
chapters.trap: PRAM is not a real machine; it ignores network delay and memory contention. Do not use it to claim a real speedup.
chapters.leave: Real topologies to Chapter 5, parallel algorithm design to Unit 2, and programming models to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: An interconnection network trades degree, diameter and bisection width, and the mesh, tree, hypercube and butterfly make different choices.
chapters.depth: Define degree, diameter, bisection width, link count and routing. Mesh: a 2D k × k mesh has degree 4 and diameter 2(k − 1). Binary tree: degree 3, diameter about 2 log₂ N, but small bisection width. Hypercube: an n-cube has N = 2ⁿ nodes, degree n, diameter n, and is recursive. Butterfly: a multistage network with n stages and fixed degree, used for permutations and fast Fourier transforms. Some syllabi add cube-connected cycle, perfect shuffle, pyramid and fully connected models; know their degree and diameter trade-offs. Include embeddings and simulation between networks, such as embedding a mesh into a hypercube and a tree into a hypercube. Do not teach sorting networks; Unit 2 covers them.

figure.aria: A three-dimensional cube drawn as two squares joined by four matching edges; each node is a 3-bit address and each edge flips one bit.

chapters.example: For N = 8 nodes, compare a 2×4 mesh, a balanced binary tree and a 3-cube. Mesh: degree 4, diameter (2 − 1) + (4 − 1) = 4, bisection width 2. Tree: degree 3, diameter 5, bisection width 1. Hypercube: degree 3, diameter 3, bisection width 4. Which has the best diameter, and which has the worst bottleneck?
chapters.trap: A small diameter is not the only measure; a tree has small degree but a bisection width of 1, so it bottlenecks.
chapters.leave: Routing algorithms and graph algorithms to Unit 2, and MPI topology mapping to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Speedup compares parallel time with one-processor time, and efficiency says how well the processors are used.
chapters.depth: Define T₁, Tₚ, p, speedup S = T₁ ÷ Tₚ, efficiency E = S ÷ p, cost = p × Tₚ, and work. Cover Amdahl's law S ≤ 1 ÷ (f + (1 − f) ÷ p), where f is the serial fraction, and the limit 1 ÷ f. Mention Gustafson's law for scaled problem size. Discuss overhead, load imbalance and communication. Explain that superlinear speedup can come only from cache or memory effects, not from the basic formula. Mention strong and weak scalability, and keep units in seconds.

figure.aria: A plot of speedup against processor count: the ideal line rises straight, while two Amdahl curves flatten, the 20 percent serial case flattening earlier than the 10 percent serial case.

chapters.example: A program takes 200 s on one processor; 20 s is serial. On 8 processors with perfect scaling of the parallel part, T8 = 20 + 180 ÷ 8 = 42.5 s. Speedup S = 200 ÷ 42.5 ≈ 4.71. Efficiency E = 4.71 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.588. Maximum speedup as p → ∞ is 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10. What limits the result?
chapters.trap: Do not use p as speedup; always use T₁ ÷ Tₚ. Also do not ignore overhead or load imbalance.
chapters.leave: Algorithm cost analysis to Unit 2, and scalability models for cloud systems to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Problem decomposition breaks work into tasks, and load balancing maps tasks to processors so that no processor stays idle too long.
chapters.depth: Cover data or domain decomposition, functional or task decomposition, recursive decomposition and pipeline decomposition. Use a dependence graph and discuss granularity. Explain mapping tasks to processors. Compare static and dynamic load balancing. Cover block, cyclic and block-cyclic distributions; master-worker; work stealing; and guided scheduling. Define makespan, idle time, load imbalance and communication cost. Use equal-task and unequal-task examples. Keep parallel algorithms in Unit 2 and operating-system scheduling separate.

figure.aria: A three-processor schedule: the first two processors run three 5 ms tasks and the third runs two tasks, so the third is idle from 10 ms to 15 ms.

chapters.example: Eight tasks of 5 ms each run on 3 processors. Static block gives Proc 1 tasks T1–T3, Proc 2 T4–T6, and Proc 3 T7–T8. Makespan = 15 ms. Total work = 8 × 5 = 40 ms. Total capacity = 3 × 15 = 45 ms. Efficiency = 40 ÷ 45 ≈ 0.889. Where is the idle time?
chapters.trap: Equal task counts do not guarantee balance when tasks have different sizes or dependencies.
chapters.leave: Parallel algorithm design to Unit 2, and distributed scheduling and coordination to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Data parallelism splits the data across devices, while model parallelism splits the model across devices.
chapters.depth: Data parallelism runs the same code on different data chunks; it matches SIMD, vector units, GPU lanes and batch splitting. In training, each replica computes gradients and an all-reduce combines them. Model parallelism splits layers or tensors across devices; pipeline parallelism sends activations between stages; tensor parallelism splits one layer. Compare when the model fits on one device, batch size, link bandwidth and pipeline bubbles. Mention hybrid parallelism. Point to pthreads and OpenMP for shared memory, MPI for distributed memory, and CUDA or OpenCL for data-parallel work; full details are in Unit 3. Include device query, thread mapping and memory hierarchy only as pointers. Use a machine-learning case study.

figure.aria: A tree splitting parallel training into data parallelism, where each GPU gets part of the batch, and model parallelism, where each GPU gets a block of layers.

chapters.example: A batch of 64 images trains a 12-layer network on 2 GPUs. Data parallel: each GPU gets 32 images and the full model. One step takes 80 ms compute plus 10 ms gradient all-reduce, so 90 ms; throughput = 64 ÷ 90 ≈ 0.711 images/ms. Model parallel: layers 1–6 on GPU 0 and 7–12 on GPU 1; each half computes in 40 ms and a 100 MB activation crosses the link in 30 ms. The first output arrives after 40 + 30 + 40 = 110 ms, then one micro-batch every max(40, 30) = 40 ms.
chapters.trap: Data parallelism needs the full model to fit on each device; model parallelism adds communication and pipeline idle time.
chapters.leave: CUDA and OpenCL syntax, thread organisation and memory hierarchy to Unit 3; distributed training on clusters to Unit 6.
